Thank you for taking this on, it's much appreciated! This will help resolve https://www.w3.org/Bugs/Public/show_bug.cgi?id=28228, a longstanding bug.

How does this relate to the `inputmode` work in #3260? Presumably if you specify both there needs to be some conflict resolution.

cc @dtapuska
Even though this has shipped already, it might be worth it to get some insights from @whatwg/a11y and @whatwg/i18n for possible future enhancements.

Some opinions from the i18n WG:

* As Addison [said](https://github.com/w3c/html/issues/208#issuecomment-346975167), among other things, there are [annoying corner cases](https://w3c.github.io/charmod-norm/#definitionCaseFolding) in case folding.

* As Richard [said](https://github.com/w3c/html/issues/208#issuecomment-347270249), different languages may need different default values, although Addison's (and Terence's) opinion in that issue was the attribute may not need to be language or input method–dependent, because it's only a hint.

For more information, please see also https://github.com/w3c/html/issues/208 and https://github.com/w3c/html/issues/1092. Thank you.

@annevk I don't believe there really is any conflict resolution for auto capitalize and what keyboard is shown... inputmode doesn't specify if the first letter should be capital. The only real conflict that comes up is if the keyboard is shown to be a numeric keyboard but that is exactly the same case as showing a default keyboard and typing the first entry as a number.

Tagging @cdumez, @rniwa 

I don't think Apple is opposed to standardizing this. The reason it's on iOS Safari but not macOS is that  iOS native interface features autocapitalization in text controls by default, but macOS doesn't. It makes sense to provide author override on iOS, but on macOS it would have no effect. 

iOS autocaplitization takes the form of making the keyboard's sticky shift key be default-on for letters where the user is expected to want a capital. This defaults to on (in sentence mode) in most text-entry contexts. The user can tap shift to choose not to capitalize the letter after all. There's no analogue for this on platforms that have a physical keyboard such as macOS. macOS does have an autocorrect

I think we don't even expose the IDL interface aspects of this on macOS or other desktop-oriented ports of WebKit, but that is likely more for historical reasons than because of being against it on the merits. We could expose the IDL attribute, have it reflect the markup attribute, and still make it have no material effect.

I have not verified whether the PR's requirements match iOS Safari behavior as intended. I am not sure which of the details and quirks described here are required for compatibility with mobile-targeted web content, either.

[1]

I may have missed it, but reading the PR source i didn't see a clear description of what autocapitalization does.  This seems to have lead to some confusion in some quarters. I see 

> assist users by automatically capitalizing the first letter of sentences

but i suspect this is slightly incorrect, since my understanding is that the browser doesn't capitalise the first letter of a sentence, but instead, as  @othermaciej says above, it sends a hint to the browser or system about how to display the visual keyboard - ie. it doesn't alter what the user typed at all. Ie. for `autocapitalize=sentence` the keyboard switches to show uppercase letters, but the user is quite at liberty to switch the keyboard back to lowercase before typing anything, so the end result is not necessarily an uppercase letter.

Is my understanding correct?  If i do have the right end of the stick here, it may be worth making that clearer (unless i missed it).

(This is handy actually, since you don't need to worry about language-specific rules for upper and lowercasing, such as whether the i needs to be a Turkish capital letter I with dot or not, which is a nest of snakes (if not familiar with that see http://rishida.net/blog/201512.html#20160907). If this is a prompt to the keyboard display, the turkish user is likely to be using a turkish keyboard and will be presented with the appropriate character.)

[2]

[OT] (i hope) The autocomplete behaviour appears to mimick the keys typed by the user in order to apply case. I assume that that is a separate thing, and it takes its cues for what to case convert from what the user typed, and that it is aware of the need to follow local case conversion rules (though i don't know whether it gets language cues for that from the system language, or from the language of the page content).

[3] 

It would be useful to be able to set an autocapitalize default at quite a high level in the document, so that it is inherited by controls that can use it, but can be overridden where necessary. One of the reasons that might be useful is...

[4] ... that some pages may want to set a default that is different from the norm, without having to set a special value on every control on the page.

For example,  Cherokee may require `autocapitalize="characters"` to be the default (for the time being), because of the font used, given that lowercase Cherokee letters have only recently been added to Unicode (that may change over time, but a good number of fonts have not yet added them).

The Georgian default should presumably be `autocapitalize="off"` by default for pages written in Georgian, given that modern Georgian text uses only lowercase letters (even though uppercase characters are encoded in the Georgian block). 

(For a little more information about Cherokee and Georgian, see http://rishida.net/blog/201512.html#20161106).

I think it would make sense to expose the `autocapitalize` IDL attribute always to make things easier for developers (then in the future they won't have to distinguish between undefined and a string value), but perhaps we change the processing model of the getter slightly so it always returns the empty string on platforms where this hint is not applicable? Or perhaps make that even more general, and say to return the empty string if the given value is not supported.

(Aside: anyone else having a hard time typing this attribute?)

One thing to keep in mind is that it's not a clear mobile/desktop split, as you can use software keyboards even on desktop platforms (e.g. I do so on my Windows 10 tablets when they are undocked). Or you can dock hardware keyboards onto phones and tablets. Indeed, you can use both at once.

Also note that the processing model outlined already has a mismatch between the "used autocapitalization hint" and the value of `el.autocapitalize`, for various reasons. So it wouldn't be too bad to have `el.autocapitalize` have some value that is meaningless on situations with hardware keyboards.

That said I don't have a real preference for what to do in such situations and am happy to defer to implementers.

I've updated the pull request to respond to the comments about formatting (I also added cross-referencing links to the attribute index), and I've tried to add some more clarity around how the attribute is typically implemented.

I haven't added anything about what the behavior should be if the attribute isn't supported. I suspect that desktop Safari might eventually want to add support e.g. to allow enabling/disabling autocapitalization for voice input (Chrome for Android currently support's the attribute for Gboard's voice input), so I don't think it makes a lot of sense to talk about "platforms where the hint is not applicable"; rather, it depends on the input method.

I will start working on the web platform tests. @othermaciej, please let us know if the Safari team would like to request changes to the behavior in the spec (or if I haven't properly documented Safari's current behavior; this would hopefully be caught once I start writing tests though).

I got a chance to work on this and update the model a bit to flow better, e.g. with less conversion between states and attributes, and a single unified "autocapitalization hint" concept. It was meant to be no normative changes, except one fix mentioned below. This brought up a couple questions:

- You stated "empty value default", but there is no such thing; there is instead "invalid value default". I made that change, which means that `autocapitalize="asdf"` will end up in the sentences state. Is that correct?
- Is this step correct, in computing the element's "own autocapitalization hint"? "If the autocapitalize content attribute is present on element, **and its value is not the empty string,** return the state of the attribute." In practice, this means the mapping of `<input autocapitalize>` just ignores the attribute (since its value is empty). Same for `<input autocapitalize="asdf">`, per the previous bullet.
- You state that the last algorithm step of "used autocapitalization hint" cannot be reached. If so, we can clean that up to something shorter. But by my reading of the editing spec, that's not the case. In particular, there are plenty of elements that are neither input/textarea elements, nor editing hosts, nor editable elements. For example, `<span contenteditable=false>` should end up in step 4. Similarly, any disconnected node, such as `document.createElement("span")`, will reach step 4. Maybe step 4 should instead say something like "If this step is reached, the element is not editable, so it has no used autocapitalization hint." Or did I misread the editing spec?

Thanks for the great PR!

Thanks for the edits! - Oops! Yes, I think you‘ve fixed it properly. The missing value default is the default state and the invalid value default is the sentences state.

> Also note that the processing model outlined already has a mismatch between the "used autocapitalization hint" and the value of `el.autocapitalize`, for various reasons.

I was wondering what these reasons were. Compatibility concerns perhaps? It seems preferable to expose the used value in the IDL attribute, if we can, though this would require modifying that computation somewhat since you'd be able to reach step 4. (At least, in my impression IDL attributes generally tend to reflect what ends up being used, if it's not too expensive.)
Yeah, that would be too far from what's implemented today, is my understanding.

There are two "mismatches" between the "used autocapitalization hint" and the value of `el.autocapitalize`. The first is that the hint doesn't match the IDL value for password, URL, and email `<input>`s.

Safari (whose behavior I wrote up in the spec) treats <input> elements of all types the same as far as IDL value. I think it passes this value to the keyboard, together with the input type, and the keyboard decides never to enable autocapitalization for password, URL, or email inputs.

There are three other possible behaviors I can think of:

- `<input>` elements of password, URL, or email always have an IDL value of "" (if the attribute is value empty or the attribute is not present) or "none" (if any other value is specified). This complicates the IDL algorithm by adding a dependency on the `<input>` type, and it's kind of weird to return "" for value empty/not present, but "none" for an overridden value. It seems the IDL attribute should either reflect what's specified, or what the used hint will be, and not some weird combination.

- `<input>` elements of password, URL, or email always have an IDL value of "none", regardless of whether or not the autocapitalize attribute is specified. This introduces an inconsistency in that `<input>` elements of other types return "" when the attribute is not specified. We could change the behavior for all <input> types so that the IDL attribute is always the used value. I think this is basically Chrome's current behavior. Note that this behavior seems to make it impossible to specify to an IME that we want the "default" behavior (the default has to be chosen by the browser-side code), so I think it's suboptimal (we could get around this problem by making the "used autocapitalization hint" not match the IDL value, but that idea's not helpful since that's what we're currently speculating about how to avoid).

- We support autocapitalize on password, URL, and email `<input>` elements the same way we do for search and text inputs. Chrome currently does this (although our default value is `none`). Chrome currently does not support inheriting the value of autocapitalize from `<form>` elements. For compatibility reasons with Safari, password, URL, and email inputs shouldn't ever inherit a non-none value of autocapitalize from their form owners. So we'd have to complicate how inheritance works to do this. The Chrome implementers believe that autocapitalization is fairly useless for these input types and would like to remove our support to match Safari, rather than complicate form inheritance.


The second "mismatch" is that for text input into an editable region, we use the IDL value from the editing host, and not any descendant element we may be inserting the text into. From one perspective, this isn't really a "mismatch," but rather just being specific about which element we're using the property from. I think it's fairly standard to get properties like autocapitalize from the editing host (e.g. I think autocomplete, autocorrect, and spellcheck are implemented the same way). It's not really feasible to try to set up a system of inheritance where any element in an editable region can override the value of autocapitalize for itself and its descendants, since a selection can span multiple elements, and then we wouldn't know which value we should use.
